titre: Triangle Shirtwaist: The Trial That Hinged on What the Owners Knew
accroche: After the 1911 fire in New York (146 dead), the owners are acquitted. The question put to the jury: did they know the door was locked?
contenu_vulgarise:
New York, Saturday, March 25, 1911, around 4:40 p.m. A fire breaks out in the Asch Building, in Greenwich Village, on the floors the Triangle Waist Company occupies from the eighth to the tenth. It kills 146 people, including 123 women and girls. The door to the Washington Place stairway is locked, among other reasons to prevent theft. The two owners are tried; they are acquitted.

## The Charge the Law Allowed

On April 11, 1911, a grand jury indicts the owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, on seven counts of manslaughter (in the second degree, according to the Cornell page). The text invoked is section 80 of the New York State Labor Code, which required that doors not be locked during working hours. The law thus existed, and it targeted precisely what had happened. But at the trial, the question put to the jurors was narrower than a closed door: did the owners know it was locked at the time of the fire?

## The Trial

The trial opens on December 4, 1911. The prosecution seeks to show that the owners knew about the lock. The defense, led by the lawyer Max Steuer, sows doubt in the jurors' minds. Steuer notably challenges the testimony of a survivor, Kate Alterman, by making her repeat it in order to suggest that the witnesses had learned their account. On December 27, twenty-three days after the opening, the jury acquits both men.

The verdict does not say these deaths were without cause. It says that, on the point put to the jurors, knowledge of the lock, the prosecution did not carry their conviction.

## What the Families Get

Twenty-three civil suits are brought against the owners. According to the timeline compiled by Cornell University, they are settled in 1914: Harris and Blanck pay $75 per life lost. Wikipedia mentions a civil judgment as early as 1913, for the same amount. In 1913 as well, Blanck is arrested for locking a door of his workshop during working hours; he is fined $20, the minimum provided, according to Wikipedia.

## The Shift

After the fire, New York State creates a Factory Investigating Commission, chaired by Robert F. Wagner, a future U.S. senator and the very man who will give his name to the 1935 Wagner Act. It drafts thirty-six labor bills, which the legislature eventually passes. A standard on doors already existed in the Labor Code, and the door was locked all the same. After the fire, the political response took the form of new laws. When a trial turns on what the accused knew, what is left for the victims?

carte.punch: 146 dead in 1911: the trial turned on what the owners knew about the door.
carte.idee: After the Triangle Waist Company fire (March 25, 1911), Harris and Blanck are tried for manslaughter under section 80 of New York's Labor Code. The question put to the jury: did they know the door was locked? On December 27, the jury acquits them.

quiz.question: On what specific point were the jurors to decide at Harris and Blanck's 1911 trial?
choix: Whether the owners had started the fire themselves to collect their insurance
Whether the building had been constructed in compliance with the city's building rules
Whether the workers had received a written warning about fire risks
Whether the owners knew the doors were locked at the time of the fire
quiz.explication: The question put to the jurors was whether the owners knew the doors were locked at the time of the fire: it was the defendants' state of mind that was at issue. The other answers describe questions that the sources consulted do not mention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did section 80 of the New York State Labor Code, invoked in 1911, say?
choix: Doors were not to be locked during working hours
Each floor was to have at least two fire extinguishers, checked every year
Fire escapes were to be painted a color visible from the street
Owners were to compensate each family of a fire victim
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Section 80 concerned doors, which were not to be locked during working hours. The other provisions cited do not correspond to what the sources describe.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Factory Investigating Commission, created in New York after the fire, draft?
choix: The rebuilding of the Asch Building at the two owners' expense
A ban on the garment-making trade in New York State
The closing of the Asch Building, declared uninhabitable by the city
Thirty-six labor bills, which the legislature eventually passed
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The commission drafted thirty-six labor bills that the legislature eventually passed. The other proposals do not correspond to what the sources describe.
